profile.title: AI & Robotics Engineer

profile.summary: AI & Robotics Engineer and Computer Engineering Master's student with proven experience in computer vision, embedded AI, and autonomous systems. Demonstrated success in deploying high-accuracy deep learning models (>97%) on edge devices such as the Raspberry Pi, and engineering TÜBİTAK-funded autonomous drone projects. Adept at bridging the gap between advanced software architectures (ROS2, TensorFlow, PyTorch) and industrial automation systems.

bullets:
Develop production firmware in Embedded C for STM32 microcontrollers powering a photoelectric smoke detector
product line, covering sensor drivers, alarm state machines and low-power operation.

Interface photoelectric smoke sensors and peripheral ICs over I2C and SPI, and implement UART and LoRa layers for
wireless alarm networking and remote device status reporting.

Designed and tuned a fuzzy logic alarm decision algorithm that separates genuine fire smoke from nuisance sources
such as cooking smoke, cigarette smoke and steam, materially reducing false alarms.

Contribute to hardware revisions through schematic design, PCB layout and pre-production circuit simulation in
Proteus, then validate firmware on the resulting boards.

Co-develop the companion Flutter mobile application for device pairing, live sensor telemetry and alarm
notifications, and define the data protocol shared between firmware and app.
experience.summary: Firmware, hardware and app work for a photoelectric smoke detector product line.
experience.problem: A smoke detector has to react to real fire immediately, stay quiet for steam and cooking smoke, and run for years on very little power.
experience.approach: I write production firmware in Embedded C for STM32 microcontrollers, interface the smoke sensors over I2C and SPI, build UART and LoRa layers for wireless alarm networks, and designed a fuzzy logic alarm decision algorithm. I also contribute to the hardware revisions and co-develop the companion Flutter app.
results: Fuzzy logic alarm decision that materially reduces false alarms
Wireless alarm networking and remote device status over LoRa
Firmware validated on new boards after each hardware revision

projects.title: AI-Powered Automated Waste Sorting System
bullets: Engineered an automated recycling system by training custom CNN models on a dataset of 12,000+ images.
Optimized memory footprint for Raspberry Pi deployment, achieving 97.69% accuracy across 5 waste streams.
Developed a ROS2 communication bridge to stream real-time inferences directly to conveyor control units.
projects.summary: A vision system beside a conveyor that recognises recyclable waste in real time on a Raspberry Pi and hands every decision to the line over ROS2.
projects.problem: Sorting mixed recyclable waste by hand is slow and inconsistent. The goal was a system that recognises each item on a moving conveyor and tells the line where it belongs — on low-cost hardware that can sit right next to the belt.
projects.approach: I trained custom CNN models on a dataset of more than 12,000 images covering five waste categories, then optimised them to run on a Raspberry Pi. A ROS2 bridge streams each prediction to the conveyor control units in real time, so the camera and the machine work as one system.

challenges.problem: A model accurate enough to sort reliably was too heavy to run in real time on a Raspberry Pi.
challenges.solution: Optimised the model's memory footprint for edge deployment while keeping 97.69% accuracy across five waste streams.

challenges.problem: Each prediction had to reach the conveyor without delay, or the item would already have passed.
challenges.solution: Built a ROS2 communication bridge that streams every inference directly to the conveyor control units.

results: 97.69% classification accuracy across 5 waste streams
Runs in real time on a Raspberry Pi
Connected to the physical conveyor automation over ROS2

projects.title: Brain Tumor MRI Analysis System
bullets: Developed an end-to-end deep learning platform for automated tumor classification and lesion segmentation.
Attained a peak accuracy of 98.43% on 2,867 clinical MRI scans using PyTorch and spatial attention.
Implemented OpenCV image processing filters to enhance soft-tissue contrast before model training.
projects.summary: A deep learning platform that classifies brain tumours and outlines the lesion on MRI scans.
projects.problem: Reading MRI scans for tumours is slow, specialised work. The aim was an end-to-end system that classifies tumours automatically and marks the lesion region, accurately enough to serve as a reliable second opinion.
projects.approach: I curated and preprocessed 2,867 high-resolution clinical MRI scans, enhanced soft-tissue contrast with OpenCV filters, and trained CNN models in PyTorch with spatial attention for tumour classification and lesion segmentation. Performance was benchmarked on precision and recall against standard medical datasets.

challenges.problem: With a few thousand images, a deep model can memorise the training set instead of learning from it.
challenges.solution: Applied robust data augmentation during training to prevent overfitting.

challenges.problem: Soft-tissue boundaries have low contrast in raw MRI scans.
challenges.solution: Added OpenCV image-processing filters that enhance contrast before training.

results: 98.43% peak tumour-classification accuracy
Trained and evaluated on 2,867 clinical MRI scans
Precision and recall benchmarked against standard medical datasets

projects.title: Bahth: Photo Search in Arabic, Turkish and English
bullets: Fine-tuned a multilingual CLIP text encoder on Arabic, Turkish and English captions, with per-language Recall@K evaluation on seen and unseen photos.
Exported the model to ONNX with int8 quantisation and built a FastAPI search service over 24,997 photos, packaged with Docker.
Built a browser demo that runs the same model with ONNX Runtime Web, including a JavaScript tokenizer checked against the Python one.
projects.summary: A multilingual image search engine: a fine-tuned CLIP text encoder that finds photos from a query typed in Arabic, Turkish or English, served by an API and running live in the browser.
projects.problem: Image search models are trained mostly on English. A compact multilingual CLIP puts the right photo first for about half of English queries, but only for a quarter of Arabic and Turkish ones.
projects.approach: I kept the CLIP image model frozen, so photo embeddings never change, and fine-tuned only the multilingual text encoder. Three training recipes were compared from the same starting point: contrastive learning on captions in three languages, distillation from the English text encoder, and both together. Every result is reported twice: on photos like the training data, and on photos the model never saw.
projects.reflection: I would train each recipe with several random seeds to put error bars on the comparison, and add Turkish sentence pairs to the distillation data, since distillation barely helped Turkish.
results: First-result accuracy (Recall@1) on Flickr8k test: Arabic 24.8% → 46.5%, Turkish 25.8% → 49.5%, English 48.9% → 60.6%
On unseen photos (XTD): Arabic 23.2% → 35.4%, Turkish 33.3% → 44.6%. About half the in-domain gain; Arabic stays the weakest language
Int8 model: 541 MB → 136 MB and about twice as fast, for 1 to 3.5 points of Recall@1
A query is answered in under 20 ms on a CPU across 24,997 photos
One training run per recipe, so differences of about a point are within noise

challenges.problem: Storing the photo embeddings as int8 changed the top results, because a few CLIP dimensions are ten times larger than the rest.
challenges.solution: I compared it with the exact ranking, found that only 80 to 88% of the top 12 results survived, and kept the embeddings in float16 instead.

challenges.problem: The text encoder was too large for a browser: 136 MB even after quantisation.
challenges.solution: I cut its vocabulary to Latin- and Arabic-script tokens, which saves 36 MB and gives identical vectors for queries in those scripts, and I load it only when a visitor types their own query.

projects.title: Lawha: Arabic Licence Plate Recognition
bullets: Fine-tuned a YOLO11n plate detector and trained a 1.3 M-parameter CRNN with CTC loss to read 17 Arabic letters and 10 digits.
Evaluated the whole pipeline end to end on 313 held-out vehicle photos, and audited every reading error against the image.
Built a browser demo where both models run on the visitor's device, so the photo is never uploaded.
projects.summary: A two-stage reader for Egyptian plates: a detector finds the plate in a vehicle photo and a second network reads its Arabic letters and digits. Both run in the browser.
projects.problem: Most open plate recognition work targets Latin plates. Arabic plates mix letters and Eastern Arabic digits, and public datasets are small and noisily labelled.
projects.approach: Two models trained on the EALPR dataset. A YOLO nano detector is fine-tuned to find plates. A small CRNN trained from scratch with CTC loss reads the cropped plate. The system is scored end to end: a plate counts only if it was found and every character is right.
projects.reflection: I would relabel the test set before reporting, and collect plates from more than one country: the model has only seen Egyptian plates.
results: Detector: 99.4% recall, 97.6% precision
Reader: 93.6% of plates read with every character right, 1.9% character error rate
End to end: 92.3% of plates found and read correctly (276 of 299)
Of the reader's 19 errors, 12 are labelling errors in the dataset by my reading of the images; the labels were not corrected and the reported number was not changed
Real plate numbers are pixelated in all published figures

challenges.problem: A plate crop and the photo it came from could end up on different sides of a random train/test split, which would inflate the score.
challenges.solution: I split the data by vehicle id, 70/15/15, and used the same split for both models.

challenges.problem: Some dataset labels are incomplete, for example a plate with four digits and three letters labelled with the digits only.
challenges.solution: I checked each of the 19 reading errors by eye and reported how many were label errors, without rescoring in my own favour.

projects.title: Harf: Handwritten Letter Recognition in Arabic, Turkish and English
bullets: Designed HarfNet, a 680k-parameter residual CNN (2.7 MB as ONNX), and trained it for Arabic and for Turkish and English letters.
Wrote a generator for the six Turkish letter classes that no public handwriting dataset covers.
Built a drawing demo in English, Turkish and Arabic that runs both models in the browser.
projects.summary: Draw a letter and a small neural network names it. Two compact CNNs, one for Arabic and one for Turkish and English, running entirely in the browser.
projects.problem: Handwriting datasets exist for Arabic and for English letters, but none covers the Turkish letters ç, ğ, İ, ö, ş and ü.
projects.approach: One residual CNN architecture, trained twice. The Arabic model learns from the AHCD dataset. The Latin model learns from EMNIST Letters plus Turkish letters that I synthesised by drawing randomised cedillas, breves and dots on real handwritten letters. Both are exported to ONNX and run in the page.
projects.reflection: I would collect a few hundred real handwritten Turkish letters, even from a handful of people, to test the synthetic classes honestly.
results: Arabic: 97.80% test accuracy on 3,360 images (the dataset's authors report 94.9%)
Turkish and English: 95.22% on 20,763 real handwritten letters
The synthetic Turkish letters score 99.4%, but on synthetic test images, not real Turkish handwriting
Known weakness: a dotless ı looks like a lowercase l, and its recall is only 59%
Each model trains in under 30 minutes on a 2-core CPU

challenges.problem: No public handwriting dataset contains ç, ğ, İ, ö, ş or ü.
challenges.solution: I synthesised them from real handwritten c, g, I, o, s and u by drawing randomised marks, and reported their accuracy separately from the real-handwriting score.

challenges.problem: Letters drawn on a canvas look different from scanned dataset letters, so a model that scores well on the test set can fail in the demo.
challenges.solution: The page keeps the strokes as vectors and redraws them at the size and stroke width the datasets use; both browser models are checked against real test images in headless Chrome.
